lessons.title: What ProteinMPNN does
lessons.summary: Inverse folding: from a backbone to sequences that should fold into it.

blocks.text: Structure prediction goes from sequence to structure. ProteinMPNN goes the other way: given a protein backbone (from RFdiffusion, a crystal structure, or anywhere else), it designs amino acid sequences likely to fold into that shape. It's a message-passing neural network (MPNN) from the Baker lab, and it's fast: designing a sequence takes about a second.

ProteinMPNN isn't a module or a single command. It's a folder of Python scripts, a git repository, installed at `/opt/ProteinMPNN`. You run its scripts with the Python from the `proteinmpnn` conda environment.

quiz.q: What does ProteinMPNN take as input, and what does it give back?
quiz.why: It's inverse folding: structure in, sequences out.

lessons.title: Running protein_mpnn_run.py
lessons.summary: The main script, its options, and its output file.

command.name: python /opt/ProteinMPNN/protein_mpnn_run.py
command.what: Designs sequences for the backbone in IN.pdb and writes them to OUT/seqs/IN.fa. Activate the proteinmpnn environment first, or Python can't find its packages.

flags: Where to write; sequences go in DIR/seqs/
Randomness: 0.1 is conservative, 0.3 more varied. Several values in quotes give several sets
Design only these chains; the others are kept as they are (the target)

blocks.tip: ProteinMPNN runs fine on a CPU for a handful of backbones. Use a GPU job for hundreds.

example.out:
>pdl1, score=1.9932, global_score=1.9932, fixed_chains=[], designed_chains=['A'], model_name=v_48_020, seed=37
MSEELLKKAEELIKRAKELGDP
>T=0.1, sample=1, score=0.8812, global_score=0.8812, seq_recovery=0.4194
MSPEELLRKAEELIRRAEELGLP
example.note: The first record is the input's own (native) sequence. Each design after it has a header with its temperature (T), sample number and score. Lower score is better: the model is more confident the sequence fits the backbone. seq_recovery is how much of the native sequence it reproduced.

quiz.q: Two designs have scores 0.85 and 1.12. Which does ProteinMPNN prefer?
quiz.why: The score is a negative log probability: lower means more likely to fit the backbone.

lessons.title: Many backbones and fixed residues
lessons.summary: The helper scripts that prepare JSONL files for bigger jobs.

blocks.text: For many backbones, or to control which positions change, you first convert the PDBs to a JSONL file (one JSON record per line) with the helper scripts in `/opt/ProteinMPNN/helper_scripts/`, then point protein_mpnn_run.py at it.

flags: Read every PDB in a folder into one JSONL file
Which chains to design (the rest stay fixed)
Residues to keep, like hotspots that must stay

quiz.q: You want to redesign a binder (chain B) but keep its three hotspot residues. Which helper do you need besides parsing?
options: make_fixed_positions_dict.py, and assign_fixed_chains.py for the chain
quiz.why: assign_fixed_chains picks the chain to design, and make_fixed_positions_dict keeps the hotspot positions unchanged.
